title: Edge model service incident runbook
summary: Use this provider-neutral runbook to triage, stabilize, recover, and verify an edge model service during an incident. It includes a remediation path for every step that can fail.
prerequisites: Access to the service's existing health signals and incident escalation route
Permission to use the service's approved traffic, capacity, and recovery controls
A documented description of the service's expected user-visible behavior

sections.title: Immediate answer and triage
paragraphs: To recover an edge model service, assign an incident owner, record the user-visible symptom and its known start time, inspect existing health signals, reduce harmful load with approved controls, restore a known-good operating state, and verify recovery with a user-visible check. If ownership cannot be established, stop nonessential changes and use the documented incident escalation route. If that route is unavailable, contact the service owner and keep the incident open rather than making unapproved changes.

This is an intermediate playbook. It assumes that you can interpret the service's existing signals and use controls that your organization has already approved, but it does not assume a particular provider, tool, version, command, or configuration.

Step 1: Record what users observe, the affected scope, the earliest confirmed time, and the incident owner. If the start time or scope cannot be established, mark it UNKNOWN, preserve the available observations, and continue with the smallest confirmed scope. If no owner accepts the incident, escalate through the documented route before making a potentially disruptive change.

Step 2: Compare the user-visible symptom with the service's existing health signals. If the signals are absent or contradictory, perform the safest existing user-visible health check and record the disagreement. If no approved check exists, do not invent one during the incident; escalate to the service owner and treat recovery as unverified.

sections.title: Stabilize and recover
paragraphs: Step 3: Use approved traffic or capacity controls to reduce harmful load while preserving the most important service behavior. If the approved control does not reduce the symptom, reverse that change when reversal is safe and return to triage. If no approved control is available, avoid improvised configuration changes, constrain exposure through an existing operational process if possible, and escalate for authorization.

Step 4: Restore the most recent known-good operating state using the established recovery process. If that restoration fails, preserve its evidence, reverse any partial change when the established process permits it, and escalate to the service owner. If no known-good state is documented, keep the service constrained and do not guess at versions, commands, or configuration values.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: Step 5: Repeat the same user-visible check used during triage and compare the relevant health signals before and after recovery. If the check still fails or the signals worsen, return to Step 2, keep the incident open, and do not declare recovery. If the result is ambiguous, mark recovery UNKNOWN and ask another authorized operator to repeat the check.

Expected evidence is an incident record containing the confirmed symptom, scope, timestamps, owner, signals reviewed, actions taken, approvals required, failed actions and their remediation, and before-and-after verification results. If any item cannot be obtained, mark that item UNKNOWN and assign a follow-up owner rather than filling the gap with an estimate.

Verify success by having an authorized operator reproduce the user-visible check and observe the relevant health signals for the service's documented observation period. If there is no documented period or baseline, recovery remains provisionally verified, the incident record must say so, and the service owner must define the missing criterion before final closure.
